action_criteria.expected_evidence: Scattered punctate and early confluent periventricular T2/FLAIR foci without basal ganglia infarcts; ventricles proportionate to sulci (Evans index 0.28); normal midbrain and pons
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude a structural, vascular or atypical-parkinsonism cause
action_criteria.rationale: PD is a clinical diagnosis; MRI is normal in PD and excludes vascular lesions, NPH, mass and the midbrain, pontine and putaminal signs of PSP and MSA [Postuma_2015]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Reduced putaminal DAT binding, left 1.12 and right 1.36 (normal >1.50), worse on the left opposite the worse right side, with preserved caudate binding: presynaptic dopaminergic deficit
action_criteria.label: Order a DaTscan (123I-ioflupane SPECT) to separate pure drug-induced parkinsonism from an underlying presynaptic dopaminergic deficit
action_criteria.rationale: Two years of metoclopramide make drug-induced parkinsonism a live alternative: the scan is normal in pure drug-induced parkinsonism and abnormal when a degenerative deficit has been unmasked [Marshall_2009]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: REM sleep without atonia in 68% of REM epochs and three episodes of kicking and arm movements with shouting on video; AHI 3.8/h; PLMI 17/h
action_criteria.label: Consider video-polysomnography for the reported dream enactment
action_criteria.rationale: Her wife describes kicking and arm flailing in sleep for 18 months; REM sleep without atonia on video-PSG would confirm REM sleep behavior disorder, a synucleinopathy marker that a D2 blocker does not cause [Berg_2015]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: UPSIT 19/40, severe microsmia: olfactory loss on a validated test
action_criteria.label: Consider a validated smell identification test for the reported smell loss
action_criteria.rationale: Olfactory loss on a validated test is an MDS supportive criterion and a feature of PD that a D2 blocker does not cause, so it supports an underlying PD unmasked by metoclopramide [Postuma_2015]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Metoclopramide flagged as a central D2 antagonist that opposes levodopa, with prokinetic options free of central D2 blockade; glipizide absorption and glucose control flagged when the prokinetic changes
action_criteria.label: Review the medication list for dopamine-blocking drugs before any dopaminergic treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Metoclopramide is a current dopamine-receptor blocker, an MDS absolute exclusion while it continues, and replacing it changes gastroparesis and glucose management [Postuma_2015]

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol or other centrally acting D2-blocking antiemetics or antipsychotics; if an antipsychotic is needed, use quetiapine or clozapine
Do not start levodopa while metoclopramide remains in the regimen
Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in older adults or in any patient with cognitive impairment
required_recommendations: Diagnose Parkinson's disease unmasked by metoclopramide: current D2-blocker exposure is an MDS absolute exclusion while it continues, but the abnormal DaTscan shows a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit that pure drug-induced parkinsonism does not cause, and RBD and hyposmia (UPSIT 19/40, severe microsmia, when tested) are not drug effects; confirm that the parkinsonism persists after withdrawal [Postuma_2015][Marshall_2009]

Stop metoclopramide, with the gastroenterologist, and manage the gastroparesis without central D2 blockade (domperidone where available after an ECG for the QTc, or short courses of erythromycin), monitoring glucose on glipizide while the prokinetic changes
Reassess after withdrawal: drug-induced signs can take weeks to months to resolve; the abnormal DaTscan shows an underlying presynaptic deficit that withdrawal will not reverse [Marshall_2009]

Once metoclopramide is stopped, if the parkinsonism persists and limits function, start carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg, half a tablet three times daily with food, increasing over 2 to 4 weeks to one tablet three times daily (300 mg/day levodopa), and review the response after 2 to 3 months; if a dopamine agonist is used, warn about impulse control disorders and excessive daytime sleepiness and ask about them at every visit [NICE_NG71]
Assess the low mood and loss of interest of the past year for a depressive disorder and treat it if present
Advise bedroom safety for the dream enactment (protect the bed partner, remove sharp objects, pad the bedside); if treatment is needed prefer melatonin, since clonazepam adds sedation and fall risk

avoided_actions.rationale: No seizure, encephalopathy or episodic confusion: EEG does not separate PD from drug-induced parkinsonism
No inflammatory, infectious or rapidly progressive feature: CSF has no role in this parkinsonism
No murmur, heart failure or cardiac symptom: an echocardiogram does not inform the parkinsonism
No palpitations, syncope or presyncope: rhythm monitoring is not indicated
Formal autonomic testing is not part of the PD work-up; bedside orthostatic measurement suffices

accepted: Parkinson's disease (idiopathic), unmasked or exacerbated by concurrent metoclopramide exposure

differential.key_features: Coexisting contributor: metoclopramide can worsen the signs, but the abnormal asymmetric DaTscan shows a presynaptic deficit that pure drug-induced parkinsonism does not produce, and dream enactment and smell loss are not drug effects; persistence after withdrawal confirms
Periventricular white matter change without basal ganglia or thalamic infarcts; asymmetric upper-limb bradykinesia with decrement, no stepwise course, and an asymmetric presynaptic deficit
May coexist: a mild bilateral postural tremor for years and a brother with ET; it does not explain bradykinesia with decrement and rigidity
No cerebellar signs, no orthostatic or urinary symptoms; normal pons and putamina on MRI
Dream enactment and parkinsonism, but no fluctuations or visual hallucinations and MoCA 25/30; the reduced household activity follows the motor slowing: no dementia
Evans index 0.28 with proportionate sulci; no urinary incontinence; upper-limb parkinsonism
Full eye movements, no falls, normal midbrain on MRI

key_clinical_evidence: Bradykinesia with decrement, slightly worse on the right, and right-predominant cogwheel rigidity, with hypomimia and hypophonia, without rest tremor: parkinsonism by the MDS entry criterion [Postuma_2015]
Metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily for 2 years, started before the 12 to 14 month motor history: current D2-blocker exposure is an MDS absolute exclusion while it continues [Postuma_2015]

DaTscan with reduced putaminal binding, left 1.12 and right 1.36 (normal >1.50), opposite the worse right side, with caudate sparing: a presynaptic deficit that pure drug-induced parkinsonism does not cause [Marshall_2009]

Dream enactment for 18 months and smell loss for a year, both beginning after metoclopramide was started: neither is a drug effect, and the UPSIT measures the smell loss (19/40, severe microsmia) [Berg_2015]
Constipation predates the motor signs but is confounded by diabetic gastroparesis
MRI with periventricular white matter change only and proportionate ventricles (Evans 0.28): no vascular, NPH or atypical-parkinsonism signature
Low mood and anhedonia over the past year: a non-motor feature to assess and treat

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Metoclopramide can worsen parkinsonism, but the abnormal asymmetric DaTscan shows an underlying presynaptic deficit and dream enactment and smell loss are not drug effects: the drug unmasks rather than explains the syndrome
red_herrings.data_point: Metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily for diabetic gastroparesis for 2 years
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor toward pure drug-induced parkinsonism and away from a neurodegenerative diagnosis

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A postural tremor may coexist, but ET does not cause bradykinesia with decrement and rigidity
red_herrings.data_point: Brother with essential tremor and her own mild bilateral postural tremor

sequence_constraints.reason: Exclude structural and vascular causes on MRI before interpreting a DaTscan [Postuma_2015]

alternatives: Domperidone 10 mg up to three times daily for the shortest possible time, where available, after an ECG
Small, frequent, low-fat, low-fibre meals for gastroparesis
contraindications: Metoclopramide with levodopa or a dopamine agonist: contraindicated in the EU product information (mutual antagonism); metoclopramide is also contraindicated in Parkinson's disease.
interactions: Metoclopramide is a central dopamine D2 receptor antagonist: it causes and worsens parkinsonism and opposes levodopa. For gastroparesis use a prokinetic without central D2 blockade, such as domperidone where available after an ECG for the QTc, or short-term erythromycin.
Metoclopramide with glipizide: faster gastric emptying alters sulfonylurea absorption and glucose control; stopping or changing the prokinetic also changes it, so monitor glucose.
Lisinopril lowers blood pressure and can add to the orthostatic effect of levodopa.
warnings: Metoclopramide: FDA boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia with treatment beyond 12 weeks.
Domperidone: QT prolongation; avoid with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and in cardiac conduction disease.
Erythromycin: QT prolongation and CYP3A4 inhibition (raises atorvastatin exposure: myopathy risk); tachyphylaxis limits it to short courses.
Metformin, omeprazole and acetaminophen: no clinically relevant interaction with levodopa.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Sunita Reddy is a 64-year-old right-handed dental hygienist presenting to the neurology clinic with a one-year history of progressive gait unsteadiness and generalized slowness of movement. Her wife, who accompanies her, first noticed that she was walking more slowly approximately 12 to 14 months ago and seemed to be shuffling her feet at times, particularly in the morning. Over the past six months, she has become noticeably slower in her daily activities, taking longer to dress, button her shirts, and complete meals. Her wife reports that her handwriting has become slightly smaller, though she attributes this to arthritis in her hands. She has had two near-falls in the past three months, both occurring when turning quickly, though she has not fallen to the ground. She denies any frank tremor, but her wife has occasionally noticed a mild shaking of her hands when she holds the newspaper up to read. She endorses some difficulty with constipation that predates her current complaints by approximately two years, as well as reduced sense of smell that she became aware of about a year ago when she could not smell a gas leak that her wife detected. She has also noticed some difficulty initiating sleep and her wife reports that she has become more restless at night, occasionally kicking and flailing her arms during sleep, which began roughly 18 months ago. Her mood has been lower over the past year; she has less motivation to engage in hobbies such as woodworking and fishing that she previously enjoyed. She was started on metoclopramide approximately two years ago by her gastroenterologist for diabetic gastroparesis with nausea and early satiety, which has improved her gastrointestinal symptoms. She takes this medication regularly three times daily. She is referred today by her primary care physician for evaluation of her progressive motor symptoms.

neurological_exam.additional: No resting tremor observed during examination, including during distraction with mental tasks (serial 7s, months of year backward). Mild postural tremor noted in both hands with arms outstretched, slightly more prominent on the right, which the patient states has been present for years. Myerson sign (glabellar tap) positive — patient fails to habituate after 10 taps. No apraxia. Writing sample shows mildly reduced letter size but no frank micrographia.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose mildly slow but accurate bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin slightly clumsy bilaterally but no clear cerebellar ataxia. Rapid alternating movements mildly slow bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, reactive to light. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Facial expression mildly hypomimic with reduced blink rate bilaterally. Mild bilateral reduction in facial expression symmetrically. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait mildly narrow-based with reduced arm swing bilaterally, more so on the right. Stride length mildly decreased. No festination. Turns require 4-5 steps. Mild difficulty with tandem gait. Romberg negative. Pull test shows 2 steps of retropulsion but self-corrects. No freezing of gait observed.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score 25/30 — lost 2 points on delayed recall, 1 point on visuospatial/executive (clock drawing with mildly impaired spacing of numbers), 1 point on verbal fluency, and 1 point on abstraction. Speech is mildly hypophonic but content and fluency are preserved. No dysarthria.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone mildly increased bilaterally at wrists with subtle cogwheel rigidity on the right slightly more than left, best appreciated with reinforcement maneuver. No frank spasticity. Strength 5/5 in all four extremities. Mild bilateral bradykinesia on finger tapping, hand opening-closing, and toe tapping — slightly worse on the right but present bilaterally. Decrement in amplitude noted after 10 repetitions bilaterally.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact throughout. Vibration mildly reduced at bilateral great toes (consistent with peripheral neuropathy, likely diabetic). Proprioception intact at toes bilaterally.
